## Overview

This unit focuses on restoration work and long-term care of young trees. Students learn that healthy ecosystems are built through ongoing care, especially in places where invasive weeds and grazing pressure can slow recovery.

## Why this matters

Restoration planting is a long-term commitment. A young tree can fail if it is crowded by weeds, damaged by grazing, or left without support. Regular monitoring helps ensure the farm becomes a more resilient and biodiverse place over time.

## Learning goals

By the end of this unit, students will be able to:

- describe why restoration work matters;
- identify common invasive weeds such as gorse;
- care for young trees and tree guards;
- record changes in plant health over time;
- explain how restoration supports biodiversity.

## Equipment

- heavy-duty gloves
- loppers or secateurs
- notebook or clip board
- boots suitable for rough ground

## Before you start

- Wear thick gloves and sturdy footwear.
- Watch your footing on slopes and uneven ground.
- Work carefully around young plants so you do not damage them.
- Never work alone in a remote or steep area.

## Task 1: Remove invasive gorse

![](images/farm-photos/farm_barn.jpg){width=60%}

Control invasive gorse to protect native plantings:

- [ ] Put on heavy-duty gloves and collect the loppers.
- [ ] Work around the hillside or restoration area carefully.
- [ ] Cut gorse back to the base and pile it neatly for disposal.
- [ ] Focus first on gorse close to young trees.
- [ ] Keep the cut material away from tree guards.

### Why this helps

Gorse competes strongly with native plants for light, space, and water. Removing it gives young natives a better chance to establish.

## Task 2: Conduct a young tree audit

Check on newly planted trees to ensure their survival:

- [ ] Walk the farm perimeter and inspect each planted tree.
- [ ] Check whether the tree is alive and whether the guard is secure.
- [ ] Remove grass and weeds inside the tree guard.
- [ ] Straighten leaning stakes and tighten loose ties.
- [ ] Note any trees that need replacement.

### Signs of a healthy tree

- green leaves or buds
- flexible stems
- healthy bark
- upright growth

### Signs of stress or failure

- brown or drooping leaves
- brittle stems
- damaged bark or broken ties
- guard leaning or rubbing the stem

## Recording observations

Help track restoration progress:

- [ ] Count the number of trees checked.
- [ ] Record how many trees are thriving, struggling, or dead.
- [ ] Note any problem areas or repeated damage.
- [ ] Take photos if there are clear changes.

## Reflection

1. Why is restoration more than just planting trees?
2. How do invasive weeds affect native plant survival?
3. What does a healthy restoration area look like?

## Extension

Create a simple restoration monitoring sheet for the class to use each month.
